summary: Describes a downgrade-resistant way for mail servers to secure SMTP transport using DANE TLSA records. It allows a gradual move of the email backbone to encrypted and authenticated TLS.

eli5.summary: Mail trucks check the address book for the right lock before delivering, so a trickster cannot make them skip the lock.

questions: what is opportunistic dane for email
what is a tlsa record for smtp
how does dane stop starttls downgrade attacks
which tlsa usage should mail servers publish
subtitle: How mail servers use DNSSEC-signed TLSA records to find out that TLS is expected, and to check the server they reach.

tldr.problem: Server-to-server email uses TLS only opportunistically, so an attacker can strip the STARTTLS offer, forge MX records, and nobody can check certificates against a sensible list of CAs.
tldr.mechanism: A mail domain publishes DNSSEC-signed TLSA records for its MX hosts. A sending server that finds usable ones must use TLS and must authenticate the server with them, or else skip that server or delay delivery.
tldr.outcome: Domains that publish TLSA records get encrypted, authenticated delivery that resists downgrade attacks. Everyone else keeps working as before, so the email backbone can move over step by step.

today: RFC 7672 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the DANE TLSA specification in RFC 6698 and the operational guidance in RFC 7671.

sections.title: Why Email Needs a New Security Model
sections.content:
Email between domains is delivered hop by hop. The destination server is found indirectly, through DNS MX records, and neither the email address nor the MX hostname says whether the sender should use encryption. So Opportunistic Security is the only workable model: use TLS when you can, and fall back to cleartext when you cannot.

RFC 7672 lists four problems with that model. First, the STARTTLS downgrade attack: the server announces TLS support in cleartext, and an attacker in the middle can simply remove that announcement. Second, without DNSSEC an attacker can forge MX replies and send mail to a server of their choice, so a certificate name check against the MX hostname proves nothing. Third, per-partner sender configuration does not scale, so it is used rarely. Fourth, relying on public certification authorities (CAs) means trusting every CA that could issue a certificate for any domain, and an unattended mail server has no user to click OK on a certificate warning.
sections.eli5: Mail trucks normally ask the mailroom, in the open, whether it has a lock. A trickster can shout over the answer so the truck thinks there is no lock. The trucks also have no good way to know whose locks to trust.

sections.title: Reading DNSSEC Results Safely
sections.content:
The client must use a security-aware resolver; security-oblivious stub resolvers MUST NOT be used. Each answer is secure, insecure, bogus or indeterminate. This RFC treats bogus and indeterminate answers, and any other lookup error such as SERVFAIL, as plain lookup failure, because they can come from lost or corrupted packets as well as from attackers.

An insecure answer is not an error. It means the zone is not signed, so the client has degraded security but delivery may go on. A proof that a record does not exist is also not an error.

If a lookup failure stops the client from learning which servers to contact, delivery MUST be delayed. If a TLSA lookup for a server fails, the client MUST treat that server as unreachable and MUST NOT deliver through it. This rule is what blocks downgrade attacks: an attacker who can only disrupt DNS can delay mail but cannot push it into cleartext.
sections.eli5: If the address book looks smudged or torn, the truck does not guess and does not hand over the letter. It waits or tries another mailroom.

sections.title: Finding the TLSA Records
sections.content:
For each server the client wants to use, it looks up a TLSA record at a name made of the port, the protocol and a TLSA base domain, for example _25._tcp.mx.example.com for port 25. The result decides what happens next.

MX records MUST be sorted by preference, and a worse-preference host with TLSA records MUST NOT jump ahead of a better-preference host without them. Loop prevention comes before channel security. If the MX set itself is insecure and DANE is mandatory for the destination, delivery MUST be delayed.

When a server name is an alias (CNAME), the client tries the fully expanded name first and then the original name as the base domain. It does the A or AAAA lookup before the TLSA lookup, and SHOULD NOT look for TLSA records if that first address answer is insecure. This avoids name servers of some large providers that mishandle TLSA queries.

A TLSA record also commits the server operator to TLS. DNSSEC-validated TLSA records MUST NOT be published for servers that do not support TLS, and the client MUST NOT deliver through such a host unless STARTTLS succeeds.
sections.eli5: The truck looks up a special page in the address book that says which lock the mailroom uses. Finding a page means the mailroom promises it really has a lock.

sections.title: Authenticating the Server
sections.content:
If at least one usable secure TLSA record is found, the client MUST use the TLSA records to authenticate the server, and MUST NOT deliver the message if authentication fails.

The RFC recommends two kinds of record. DANE-EE(3) pins the server's own certificate (or its key). It is the first choice, as DANE-EE(3) SPKI(1) SHA2-256(1). With it, the client MUST NOT perform certificate name checks, and the certificate's expiry date MUST be ignored, because the validity of the binding comes from the DNSSEC signature. DANE-TA(2) publishes a trust anchor (an issuing CA) instead, with Cert(0) and SHA2-256(1) as the second choice. Here the client MUST check names, using the TLSA base domain as the primary reference identifier. When the base domain came from a secure MX lookup, the original next-hop domain is a second reference identifier. Servers using DANE-TA(2) MUST send the trust anchor certificate in the TLS handshake chain.

The PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) usages SHOULD NOT be published for port 25 SMTP. Clients cannot be expected to hold a complete CA list, and an attacker who can break DNSSEC could replace those records anyway. Clients MAY treat them as unusable.
sections.eli5: Either the mailroom shows the exact lock the book describes, or it shows a lock made by a locksmith the book names. Either way, if the lock does not match, the letter stays on the truck.

sections.title: Rolling Keys and Publishing Safely
sections.content:
Before a server starts using a new key or certificate, two TLSA records MUST be published: one for the current key and one for its replacement. Only after the old records have expired from DNS caches should the server switch. Once the new key is in use, the old record can be removed. Removing a record from DNS is also how a compromised key is revoked, so clients do not need CRL or OCSP support.

With DANE-TA(2), servers can point their TLSA names by CNAME at a shared record. If one server's key is compromised, its CNAME SHOULD be replaced with a DANE-EE(3) association until that certificate expires.

Publishers also have rules. Servers that enable STARTTLS only for clients that retried after greylisting MUST NOT do so if they also want to support DANE, because DANE clients will never make the initial cleartext attempt. Publishers should follow the TLSA guidance in RFC 7671 for digest algorithm agility, record size, TTLs and signature lifetimes.
sections.eli5: When you change the lock, you first add the new lock's picture to the address book next to the old one, wait until everyone has seen it, and only then change the real lock.

sections.title: Mandatory DANE and Operations
sections.content:
A sender may require DANE for chosen destinations, for example when it sends sensitive mail or has regulatory duties. With mandatory DANE TLS, if no usable TLSA records are found, delivery is delayed, so mail is only sent over an authenticated TLS channel. Such administrators need to watch their logs and queues: if a partner misconfigures TLSA records, disables DNSSEC or breaks its certificate chain, mail will be delayed and may bounce.

For interoperability, the client MUST send the TLS SNI extension containing the TLSA base domain. Servers MUST NOT insist on SNI, and when SNI is missing or unknown they MUST send some fallback certificate chain. An implementation MAY offer an audit-only mode that logs a failure and continues at lower security, but unless local policy says so, a client MUST NOT deliver through a server whose chain fails to match a usable TLSA record.
sections.eli5: Some senders say they will only deliver to mailrooms that prove their lock. If a mailroom breaks its own paperwork, those letters wait in a pile until it is fixed.

sections.title: What It Protects and What It Does Not
sections.content:
For domains that sign their MX records and publish signed TLSA records, sending servers can securely learn both that TLS is available and how to authenticate the destination. The RFC does not claim to secure all SMTP traffic, since that is not practical until DNSSEC and DANE adoption are universal. It coexists with the existing insecure mail backbone and with manually configured TLS arrangements.

The scheme depends critically on DNSSEC. If DNSSEC is compromised, there is no public-CA fallback, and an attacker could publish usage 3 associations. Implementations must strictly follow the rules that say when a server must be considered unreachable, so that they never start a cleartext or unauthenticated connection when they should not.

The RFC also notes that MUA-to-MSA submission could use similar rules with SRV records, but leaves that to future documents.
sections.eli5: The tamper-proof address book is the one thing everyone must trust. If someone breaks into it, the whole scheme fails, so the trucks must follow the rules exactly.

viz.caption: WHAT THE CLIENT DOES WITH EACH TLSA LOOKUP RESULT (RFC 7672)

cells: Secure, at least one usable record
MUST use TLS and authenticate the server; on failure try the next server or delay
MUST use TLS, no authentication required; on failure try the next server or delay
Insecure, or authenticated denial of existence
SHOULD use pre-DANE opportunistic TLS, cleartext allowed
MUST try the next server or delay delivery

viz.caption: TLSA CERTIFICATE USAGES AND HOW RFC 7672 TREATS THEM

items.label: DANE-EE(3)
items.desc: Match the server's own certificate; no name checks; expiry ignored. First choice.

items.label: DANE-TA(2)
items.desc: Match a trust anchor in the chain; name checks required. Second choice.

items.label: PKIX-TA(0)
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be published for port 25 SMTP; may be treated as unusable.

items.label: PKIX-EE(1)
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be published for port 25 SMTP; may be treated as unusable.
